Mood Ring
MOOD ring
noun (Boomer slang)
Invented in 1975 by Josh Reynolds and Maris Ambats in New York: a ring set with a clear stone over a layer of thermochromic liquid crystals that change color with temperature, sold with a chart claiming that each color reveals the wearer’s mood (blue for calm or happy, black for stressed, and so on). Millions were sold in 1975–76; the fad faded by the end of the decade and has returned periodically as a nostalgia item.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A mood ring was a 1975 novelty: a ring whose stone changed color with the warmth of your finger, supposedly showing whether you were calm, happy, nervous, or angry. Millions of teenagers checked their rings to find out how they felt, and checked their dates’ rings to find out how they felt about them. The Christian observation: the fad is funny, but it reveals a deep wish — to have the heart made readable — and a deep confusion about where to look. A mood ring reads skin temperature, not the soul. Scripture says the heart cannot be read so easily, even by its owner: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jer 17:9). Only God can: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts" (Psa 139:23). "The LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). The mood ring also reflects the 1970s turn toward feelings as the truest thing about a person — the mood as the self. Scripture asks the believer to rule his moods rather than be ruled by them: "He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls" (Pro 25:28), and "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" (Pro 4:23). A child can enjoy a mood ring as a toy. But his parents can teach him that God knows his heart better than any stone, and that he is more than the color of his feelings today.

Webster 1828 Definition

1975 novelty ring (Reynolds and Ambats) whose heat-sensitive stone changed color, supposedly revealing the wearer’s mood — a wish to read the heart that Scripture reserves to God (Jer 17:9; Psa 139:23), with a call to rule one’s spirit (Pro 25:28).

MOOD RING, n. (1975; Boomer era fad) A ring with a stone containing thermochromic liquid crystals that change color with temperature, popularly claimed to indicate the wearer’s emotional state.

Webster (1828) — MOOD, noun [Latin animus.] 1. Temper of mind; temporary state of the mind in regard to passion or feeling; humor; as a melancholy mood; an angry mood; a suppliant mood 2. Anger; heat of temper. [In this sense Little Used , unless qualified by an adjective.]

Decode for families: today’s apps that track your mood are the mood ring with a subscription.

Key Scripture

Jer 17:9 — "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"

Psa 139:23 — "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:"

1Sa 16:7 — "But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."

Pro 25:28 — "He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls."

Modern Corruption

The mood ring promised to make the heart readable and treated mood as the self; Scripture says only God searches the heart and calls the believer to rule his spirit, not to be ruled by it.

expand to see more

The mood ring was harmless as a toy, but it belonged to a decade that was learning to treat feelings as the deepest truth about a person. "How do you feel about it?" replaced "Is it right?" as the moral question, and the mood ring was the cheerful jewelry of that shift. Two generations later, we have apps that track moods and a culture that treats every feeling as a fact to be affirmed. Scripture’s Jer 17:9 is the corrective: the heart is not a reliable narrator.

There is also a gentle superstition in the fad: a stone that tells you something about yourself. Many teenagers half-believed it. The Christian learns to look elsewhere — to the God who searches hearts (Psa 139:23) and to His Word, which is "a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." That is a mirror worth checking.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English mód (mind, spirit, temper) + ring → 1975 mood ring (thermochromic liquid crystal novelty).
